Every corner adds up to one full lap, 360°, so corner = 360 ÷ sides.

A new shape in the code is just two edits: the range(...) count and that corner angle.


Elicit the 360 with bodies first, not algebra: one student walks a triangle on the mat and ends facing the way they started — however many corners, the turning always totals one full spin. Then drive the demo from their guesses: pick Triangle, each corner flashes its 120° turn right on the shape while the dial climbs 120 → 240 → 360 and closes; pick Octagon, eight skinny 45s stack to the same 360. That “always lands on 360” is the whole proof — corner = 360 ÷ n falls out of it. The contrast with the morning is worth a beat: same octagon, but the gyro eats robot-degrees directly, so the gap ÷ wheel translation retires (it returns at the D8 reveal inside DriveBase). Every squad edits their own file to a triangle and runs it before Shape Shifter.

⏱️ Time: 20 minutes

title: Drive a Square
text:
Shape Shifter 🔺⬛⬣






The challenge


The judge calls a shape, triangle up to octagon. 60 seconds to edit and run: range(?) plus corner = 360 ÷ sides. Score = gap from tape to finish, tiebreak = fewest lines touched. 3 calls, best two count.




Two edits per shape. That’s the whole race. Copy-pasters meet their doom at the octagon. 😈
Pro question: which drifts more, 3 fat corners or 8 skinny ones? Watch your traces and keep the answer for tomorrow.


Uses exactly today’s material: for + range, the watched-turn while, 360 ÷ n, and heading — no def; that arrives tomorrow. The 60-second edit window is the point: a loop makes a new shape a two-number change, so the octagon call separates loopers from pasters on the clock. The closure gap keeps the coast visible — 8 corners × ~4° beats 3 × ~4°, so the octagon drifts more; squads that see that are already leaning into tomorrow’s cure. Coach scorecard: edit discipline (two calm edits vs. a rewrite), 360 ÷ n reasoning without a calculator, and who re-tapes and re-tests between calls.

title: Drive a Square
text:
Today’s gate






You’re done today when…


The judge calls any shape → your loop draws it with watched corners (two edits, no copy-paste). You can explain heading, walk your watched turn line by line, and name who’s guilty for the 94.




Tomorrow: the coast meets its cure, which is to arrive slowly. Then the cure gets a brain: speed that shrinks with the error. One formula, and it has a name every roboticist knows.

title: Gears & Grippers
text:
Feel it: the heavy lift 🏋️

Clamp something heavy, like a full water bottle. Lift.
What happens? Why? The motor is trying its hardest, so where is the strength going?



The motor isn’t weak. The ratio is. Your gears hand the claw exactly the strength the motor makes, 1 : 1.



The engineered failure that makes gear theory land as a rescue instead of a lecture. With the 1:1 bevel pairs, a genuinely heavy object slips or stalls the medium motor — let them feel it strain, and don’t let a stall cook the motor for more than a moment. Then the hook question: “a car engine can’t lift a car either — yet the jack in the trunk lifts it with one hand. What’s the trick?” Someone will say gears or leverage — that someone just introduced Act B for you.

title: Gears & Grippers
section: Break it: two claws, one brain 🧠
text:
Break it: two claws, one brain 🧠

Carry the bottle in the top claw. Now open the bottom claw without moving the top one.
Try. What happens? Is this a feature or a bug?



Both. One motor → two claws is a motor saved, and 4 motors is the Elementary cap (§5.2.8). The price is that they always move together. Engineering is knowing the price. 🏷️



The coupling discovery, on their own design decision. Name the budget correctly, because this is where it is usually got wrong: our robot has a spare port (A); what it does not have is a spare motor — F and B drive, E and C grip, and Elementary allows 4, maximum (§5.2.8). A second gripper motor is what we cannot afford, not a second plug.
Praise the trade before naming its cost, then plant the question that decides whether the price is affordable: does any moment in the anchor run need “top claw holding” AND “bottom claw moving” at once? Have squads check against the cables → mic sequence. If yes, the fixes are geometry (each claw engages in a different part of the rotation range) or making one claw passive — a design conversation for the build block. Point at the build itself: have a squad trace motor shaft → axle → gear pair → claw arm with a finger, and the coupling is right there in their hands.

title: Gears & Grippers
text:
Count teeth, know the future

Every gear question starts the same way: count the teeth.
Ratio = follower teeth ÷ driver teeth.



  
  
  
  
  
  in: 1 turn
  
  
  
  out: 1 turn
  
  
  
  20T
  20T
  bevel pair: 90° corner
  
  follower ÷ driver
  20 ÷ 20 = 1 : 1
  same speed · same strength
  all it buys: the 90° corner




Bevel gears buy direction, not strength. Your gripper spent its gears on the corner, so the lift failed.




Teeth = size: meshing gears share tooth size. It’s a ratio, so unlike the wheel, π cancels. Just count. 🔢



Keep the arithmetic tiny: teeth in, teeth out, one division. Have every squad physically count the teeth on a spare bevel gear — counting beats being told. The reveal sentence is the punchline of Act A: their gear pair spends its entire budget on turning the axis 90° (which the build needs — motor lies flat, claws swing on vertical axles) and has nothing left for strength. Now the fix is obvious before it’s taught: change the ratio.

title: Gears & Grippers
text:
The trade: speed ⇄ strength

  
    driver 24T → follower:
    12T
    24T
    36T
  
  
    DRIVER 24T
    FOLLOWER
    
      
      
      
      
      
    
    
      
      
      
      
      
    
  
  




Small drives big → slower but stronger. Speed and strength are one budget, and gears decide how to spend it.


Click through the three followers and narrate the yellow spokes — the driver is always the 24T, only the follower changes. 12T: the claw spins twice as fast and grips half as hard. 24T: exactly the motor, no bonus — the same 1:1 deal their own bevel pair gives them. 36T: gives up a third of its speed and buys half again the strength (×1.5). One sentence carries the slide: “speed and strength are the same budget — gears just move money between the accounts.”
Then link each direction to a mission verb: gear for torque where a push needs force (cable pusher against friction), for speed where it needs reach (a claw that must open wide in a hurry). Physical demo beats the animation if time allows: hold a 12T driving a 36T between two fingers and feel the follower resist. Resist the full gear zoo — idlers, racks, worms and compound trains are continuation-season material. Coach prep: WRO-Learn Fundamentals of Mechanics, PrimeLessons Robot Designs, Competition Ready L7 Time for an Upgrade.

title: Gears & Grippers
text:
Challenge: tune YOUR gripper 🛠️






Pick one, 20 minutes



💪 Stronger: re-gear so the bottle lift succeeds, and prove it with the lift
⚡ Faster: re-gear so open→close beats the stopwatch, and prove it with a timed cycle





Rules: same motor, same port, only the gears change
Still fits the 250 mm cube with claws closed 📏
Before you build: say the ratio out loud. Predict, then prove


Modification is their proven skill — this stretches it one step, with a prediction gate (“say the ratio before you touch a gear”) so the theory does the work. Squads choose their own goal; both choices are correct, which quietly teaches that gearing is a decision, not an answer. Watch for the classic trap: gearing so slow the claw takes 5 seconds to close — a run costs time. If a squad finishes early: “now make the two claws close at different speeds from the same motor” — a compound ratio discovered, not assigned. This is also where mechanism talent becomes visible post-draft; watch who leads the rebuild.

50 of the ~135 anchor, with zero color needed. You’ve already shoved cables with the bare chassis. Now the claw makes it repeatable.



Both lines come from the game rules via the plan’s scoring table — the operative word in both is upright, and upright is decided by mechanism geometry + approach angle, not by code. The mission previews planted this: squads already discovered that approach angle decides whether a shoved cable stands or falls. Map the two jobs onto their own two claws: the bottom sweep claw is a natural cable pusher, the top carry claw a natural mic carrier — the design was pointed at these tasks all along; today they find that out.

title: Gears & Grippers
section: Pusher physics: three tricks that beat luck
text:
Pusher physics: three tricks that beat luck


  
  
  
  
  
  
  robot
  
  ③ geared for force
  
  
  
  ① funnel: it centers itself
  
  
  cable
  
  
  
  
  aim error ±5 mm
  
  
  
  ② push PAST the line
  
  
  
  then back off
  GREY AREA




Design rule: let the mechanism forgive what the driving can’t guarantee. ±5 mm of aim error should still score.



This slide is the difference between a build that works once and a mechanism that gates at ≥8/10. The funnel is tolerance engineering a 9-year-old can hold: the robot will never arrive perfectly, so build a mouth that makes imperfect arrivals perfect enough. Over-travel is its twin in code. Pros design the mechanism around the worst expected approach, not the best. The ±5 mm number is a design target to test against, not a rule — nudge their aim off on purpose and see if the funnel saves it. The third trick is the gear challenge coming home: torque where the push needs force, speed where the claw needs reach.

title: Gears & Grippers
section: Break it: the claw that got shoved 💥
text:
Break it: the claw that got shoved 💥

Close the claw. Now shove it back open with your hand, with the program still running.
Two squads, same nudge, one word different:
gripper.run_angle(300, 150)     # squad A
gripper.run_target(300, 150)    # squad B
Run it again. Do the two claws land in the same place? 👀



No. Squad A is 150° past the shove. Squad B went back to the same spot it always uses.
Same nudge. One verb forgave you. 🤔



Five minutes, and it must be felt, not told — the slide dies if you announce the answer. Get real predictions on the board first; most of the room will guess both claws end up wrong, because “I moved it with my hand” feels like it must break something. Then the reveal question: counts from where, exactly? run_angle counts from here — wherever the claw happens to be the instant the line runs, nudge included. run_target counts from a zero, and does not care how the claw got where it is. Do NOT resolve which is “better” yet — that’s the next slide, and it lands harder as a table they fill in.
Two staging notes. Keep the program running (a loop with a button wait, or the REPL) — that is what makes squad B recover. And make the shove big and obvious, 30–40°; a 5° nudge looks like noise. If a squad’s claw is heavily geared down, their hand-shove may back-drive the gears rather than the motor — have them nudge the motor’s own axle instead.

title: Gears & Grippers
text:
Move by, or move to 📐









run_angle(300, 150)
run_target(300, 150)




you say
“turn 150° more”
“go to 150”


counts from
wherever it is right now
zero


run it twice
moves again, 300 total
second one does nothing


after a shove
inherits the shove ❌
drives it back out ✅





You already own this pair. robot.turn(90, absolute=True) is a compass. run_angle is a steering wheel. 🧭
Wheels roll forever, so by is fine. A claw has a place it must be, so mechanisms use run_target.




⚠️ run_target ignores the sign of the speed. The target decides the direction. run_target(-300, 0) and run_target(300, 0) do the same thing, so to go the other way, change the target, not the speed.



Build the table live, one row at a time, from what they just watched. Row 3 is the cheapest to prove and the most convincing: run either line twice and run_angle walks the claw across the room while run_target sits there refusing to move because it has already arrived.
The absolute-turn callback is the sentence of the slide, and it is a genuine callback: the square day taught exactly this on the gyro, and the checkpoint’s hardest question turned on it. Say the general rule out loud, because it is the transferable one: a relative move inherits every mistake before it; an absolute move forgets them. That is also why movements.py deliberately has no “turn 90 from here” verb.
The purple fragment is a real trap that costs an afternoon, because every other verb they own — run_angle, run, run_until_stalled — taught them “negative means the other way”, and this one quietly doesn’t. Show it: run_target(-300, 0) from an open claw closes it, exactly like the positive version, because 0 is on the same side either way.

title: Gears & Grippers
text:
So whose zero is it? 💥

run_target goes to 150. 150 measured from where?
Not from your jaws. From a mark on the motor shaft, picked by the hub the moment your program started.
Slip one gear tooth and the shaft mark stays put. Your jaws don’t.



You re-geared this claw an hour ago. Every angle in your notebook is now measured from a mark that moved. 😱



The code was never wrong. The zero was never yours. 🎯


This is the beat that earns home(), so don’t rush it — and it is a different failure from the shove two slides back, which is the point. A shove gets counted; the motor was awake and watching. What is not counted is anything that changes the relationship between the motor shaft and your jaws: a gear tooth skipping under load, an axle pulled and re-seated one notch round, and above all a re-gear, which is a thing this room did to itself this morning. Stage the cheapest version: pull the claw axle, put it back one tooth over, re-run the exact same line, watch the jaws land somewhere new with no edit to the code. Thirty seconds, impossible to argue with.
Say the ownership line slowly, because it is the whole argument: zero is a mark on the motor, and the motor has never seen your claw. That mismatch is fine right up until something between the two moves, and then it is silent, because a wrong zero produces perfectly confident wrong behaviour. Passes on the bench, dies on the mat, no error message.
Then hold the room in it. Do not give the fix. Someone will say “can’t it just find zero by itself?” — that sentence is the next slide, in their words, and it is worth waiting twenty seconds of silence for.

title: Gears & Grippers
section: home(): go and touch your zero 🧱
text:
home(): go and touch your zero 🧱
def home():
    """Shut on nothing. THAT is zero."""
    claw.run_until_stalled(-CLOSE_SPEED, then=Stop.COAST, duty_limit=___)
    wait(200)                    # let the gears unwind before we believe it
    claw.reset_angle(___)        # jaws met = 0 -- every run, every robot
    claw.run_target(OPEN_SPEED, READY_ANGLE, then=Stop.COAST)



Part
What it means




speed
which way and how fast, where negative = the other way


then=Stop.COAST
relax when you arrive


duty_limit
how hard it may push, 0–100. Start at 40





Why shut and not open? Because “did I catch it?” is a question about the jaws meeting. Put your zero where the question is, and the answer is just “did we stop before 0?” 🎯



Blanks: duty_limit=40 and reset_angle(0). They already own run_until_stalled from the wall day, so the table is a reminder, not a lesson — spend the time on the datum instead.
The teal fragment is the whole slide. The claw could home either way; homing shut is the choice that deletes a number. Zero at fully-open means “did I catch something?” can only be answered against a measured landmark — how far away the jaws meet — which is a number you must measure, re-measure after every re-gear, and which is silently wrong in between. Zero at jaws met makes that number 0 by construction, so it cannot be mis-measured or go stale. Say the portable version: put the zero where the question is. This is the same move as find_line() for the wheels — stop guessing, go and touch something that is where it says it is — and the contrast is worth naming: the claw has a hard stop it can press against, so home() is exact; the mat only offers landmarks to look at, so find_line() fixes distance and nothing fixes heading.
Line 4 is the one they’ll want to delete — make them keep it. The gear train is still under load the instant the stall is detected, and reading the angle before it unwinds bakes a few degrees of backlash into zero, every run, in the same direction. Systematic error, not noise, and systematic errors survive into competition. Line 6 is why the claw ends up open and ready rather than clamped shut — READY_ANGLE is a number they choose (wide enough for the biggest thing they carry), not one they measure.
Assign it now as a hard habit: home() is line one of every mission program from today onward, no exceptions, enforced at the gate. It costs one second.

title: Gears & Grippers
text:
Try to break the homing 🔨

Four ways it goes wrong. Stage each one.








Break it
What you see




home the wrong direction
zero lands at open, and nothing closes again


duty_limit too high
you hear the teeth skip, a stripped gear 🔊


duty_limit too low
zero lands somewhere new, so homing is a lie


skip the wait(200)
zero drifts, always the same way





Every one of these passes on your desk. That’s why you stage them on purpose. 🎭



Squads split the four and stage them for each other — a competition-grade debugging drill, not a demo, so protect ten minutes for it.
Supervise the duty_limit rows. Let them hear a real skip at duty_limit=100 on a re-geared claw once, briefly, then stop it; the sound is worth more than any warning, and it’s the same lesson the heavy-lift break-it opened the day with — torque has consequences at both ends of the chain. Do not let anyone sit at 100 for more than a second, and don’t run this on a build you can’t afford to re-teeth. The low side is subtler and more valuable: at 15 the jaws stop short of actually meeting, reset_angle(0) fires anyway, and now zero is almost right — worse than obviously wrong, because it passes on the bench and fails on the mat. Tie it back: a tuning knob found by feel, exactly like KP.
Say the scope line deliberately — duty_limit lives in home() and nowhere else, because it is a percentage of whatever power is available today, which is the same objection they already accepted against dc(). Finding a rigid stop can afford that sloppiness; deciding how hard to squeeze an object cannot. That distinction is the hinge the rest of the session turns on.
The wrong-direction row is the most common: they flip a sign, the claw homes to open, zero lands at the wrong end of the travel, and every grab() afterwards asks the motor to drive somewhere it already is. It reconnects to the sign rule in their gripper file — positive must mean opening, and if it doesn’t, you flip Direction, not the numbers. Collect the four “what you’d see” answers on the board — that list is a diagnostic sheet for the rest of the season.

title: Gears & Grippers
section: Break it: the claw that lets go 💥
text:
Break it: the claw that lets go 💥

Grip it by stalling. Then take the robot for a ride.
gripper.run_until_stalled(-300, then=Stop.HOLD, duty_limit=50)
drive_straight(600)
robot.turn(90, absolute=True)
The claw never opened. So how did the bottle get out? 🍾



Stalling stopped where it stopped, then held that spot. The bottle settled 1 mm, and the squeeze went to zero. 😱



Ten minutes, and it has to be felt — this is the break-it the whole grip arc hangs on, and the failure they will otherwise meet for the first time in front of a judge. Everyone grips by stalling, everyone drives, and most claws will shed the object on the turn; if a squad’s doesn’t, have them tap the object once mid-carry, or use something rounder.
Sit in the confusion before explaining: the claw is visibly still closed, the code visibly never opened it, so the object cannot be gone — and yet it is. The reveal is the difference between HOLDING A POSITION and HOLDING A FORCE, worth drawing on the board: Stop.HOLD after a stall means “stay at this angle”, so the instant the object shifts a hair, the error is zero, the motor relaxes, and the claw is merely resting on the object. Ask what the motor would have to do instead to keep pressing — someone will say “keep closing”, and that is the next slide, in their words.
Do not let the session frame stalling as bad — it is still exactly right for home(), and the distinction (rigid frame vs. a squashy object that moves) is the transferable idea.

title: Gears & Grippers
section: Grip is a force, not a place 🤝
text:
Grip is a force, not a place 🤝
claw.control.limits(torque=___)      # the squeeze -- set ONCE

def grab():
    close_and_watch(CLOSE_SPEED, GRIP_TIMEOUT_MS)   # lean in until it bites
    return holding()        # no hold(), no stop() -- that IS the squeeze


close_and_watch aims at GRIP_TARGET, a few degrees past where the jaws meet. It can never get there, and that’s the point. It never stops trying. 🎯




Never call hold() here. A motor that arrives stops pushing. 🚫



Blank is torque=GRIP_TORQUE, and the units matter: mNm, an amount of real turning force, not a percentage. Make them say why that beats duty_limit — they already accepted the argument about dc(), and this is the same argument in a different hat: a percentage is a promise about the battery, a unit is a promise about the robot.
Teach the aim-past trick with hands, not words: hold a squad’s claw half-closed and ask one student to keep squeezing while you slowly let the object shrink. To keep pressure they have to keep moving, which is exactly what an unreachable target buys. And note that the unreachable target is now trivially easy to state — zero is where the jaws meet, so “past the jaws” is just a small negative number, the same in every squad’s file.
close_and_watch is the one piece of plumbing worth a sentence, not a slide: it starts the move with wait=False and watches for three ways out — found the object, found nothing, or jammed — with a timer so a jam costs 1.5 seconds instead of the rest of the run. Open the file if anyone asks; don’t spend the room’s attention on the loop.
The purple fragment is the trap they will otherwise fall into: several will “tidy up” by adding claw.hold() at the end, which silently restores the exact bug the previous slide staged. Say it out loud: the move is left running on purpose. Contrast with lift_gripper.py if anyone built a fork — a fork asks for a height and means it, because gravity does the holding, so position control is right there and wrong here. Same verbs, opposite reasoning.

title: Gears & Grippers
text:
Did you actually catch it? 🎣



jaws stopped
load
what happened




at 0, they met
high
closed on air 🌬️


short of 0
high
holding it ✅


short of 0
low
it’s gone 👻



def holding():
    if claw.angle() < ___:        # jaws met -- nothing in them
        return False
    return grip_load() > ___


One signal can’t do it. The angle can’t tell a held bottle from one that fell out a second ago. 📏




So ask the same question twice. 🚚
claw.grab()                 # got it HERE?
drive_straight(600)
if not claw.holding():      # still got it THERE?
    print("dropped it, skip the placing")



Blanks are AIR_MARGIN (start at 20) and GRIP_LOAD_MIN (start at 60 mNm, then measure). Walk the truth table row by row and make them supply the third row themselves — rows one and two are the obvious ones, row three is the one that pays.
Notice how little there is to hold in your head now: the jaws meet at 0, so “closed on air” is just “angle near zero” and AIR_MARGIN is the only slack you have to choose. There is no measured empty angle to look up, to get wrong, or to re-measure after this morning’s re-gear.
The move to teach here is that it is the same function, asked twice. There is no second verb, and deliberately isn’t one: a still_holding() wrapper existed for exactly one season and did nothing but call holding(), which taught the room that two names meant two behaviours and sent students hunting for a difference that was never there (#40). “Ask it again later” is a habit, and habits belong in the mission list where the student can see the second call.
Why asking late is possible at all is the dividend from the previous slide: because grab() leaves the claw actively squeezing, the load reading stays meaningful for the whole carry. Under a stall-and-hold grip the motor had already relaxed, so “do I still have it?” had no signal to read. That is competition thinking arriving early — a run that discovers an empty claw before the placing manoeuvre skips it and banks the time. Get every squad to add the second call to one mission leg today.
Nice bonus if you have a minute — ask what holding() should say for a squashy object versus a rigid one, and let them find that both margins are TUNE knobs, not constants handed down.

title: Gears & Grippers
text:
Ten grabs, not one 🔬

Run grip_test.py. Same object, same claw, ten times.
Then write your spread on the board, not your angle.




spread
verdict




under 10°
build a run on it ✅


10–25°
your claw rocks in its mounting 🔧


over 25°
fix the build, not the code 💀





It also grabs five times by stalling, right next to five by torque. Don’t take my word for it, read the two spreads. 📊



One reading always looks fine, so a single number cannot tell you whether your claw is competition-grade. Spread can. Make the board column say spread, not angle — the room comparing spreads is a completely different conversation, because a wide spread is a build defect and points at a specific fix (the claw rocks, the mount flexes, the object rolls before the jaws arrive) rather than at a number to fiddle with. Hold the line on the bottom row when someone wants to tune their way out of a 30° spread.
The angle column is now directly readable: it is how far the object holds the jaws open, measured from shut. So the smallest number in the table is also the answer to “where does AIR_MARGIN go?” — comfortably under it. That is the only number the test asks them to write down, besides GRIP_LOAD_MIN.
Budget: about two minutes per squad, and they should run it more than once — ideally now and again at the end of the day on a tired battery, which is what makes the stall-versus-torque column honest. If the two spreads come out close on a fresh battery, say so plainly rather than overselling; the effect grows as the battery sags, and a coach who oversells a result the students can see is fine loses the argument they actually need to win.

title: Gears & Grippers
section: Two new jobs, and no new verbs 📦
text:
Two new jobs, and no new verbs 📦
# the cable -- push PAST the line, then leave it standing
robot.turn(CABLE_UPPER_HEADING, absolute=True)
drive_straight(TO_CABLE_MM + ___)     # over-travel: how far past?
drive_straight(-BACKOFF_MM)

# the mic -- arrive, let go GENTLY, retreat
drive_straight(TO_MIC_MM)
claw.let_go()                         # a spring-open claw tips it over
drive_straight(-BACKOFF_MM)


Every line is a verb you already own. Six lines, zero defs: these are list entries, not library. 🗂️




Tempted to call it push_cable()? Ask the wrapper test: does the name buy a new behaviour, or just hide three lines you can already read? 🧐



The blanks are the point — the structure is given (their level), the numbers are theirs to find (the stretch): over-travel ≈ 20–30 mm, found on the mat, not chosen at the desk; and LET_GO_TRAVEL in CLAW FACTS is what makes the mic land upright, because a claw that springs all the way open knocks it over and “upright” is where the 20 points live.
The slide’s real move is the one it refuses to make. Last season these six lines were handed over as push_cable() and place_mic(), and that was wrong for the same reason still_holding() was wrong: a name that wraps three calls you can already read buys you nothing and costs you the ability to see the run. Expect someone to propose the wrapper — they should, it’s the habit we drilled — and answer with the wrapper test on the slide. drive_straight earns its name (it hides the DriveBase settings dance); push_cable doesn’t (it hides a turn and two drives). Say plainly that this is a deferral, not a ban: when they have retyped the same three lines in four missions, that is the day the name is earned — in the continuation season, with the mission dictionary.
Filing rule: driving verbs live in movements.py; home, grab, release, let_go and holding live in a gripper file — claw_gripper.py and/or lift_gripper.py, one per mechanism the robot actually carries; the cable and the mic live in the mission program, as steps, because they are the mission and nothing else.

⏱️ Time: 10 minutes

Recap by asking: name the verbs, who tuned what, which constant fixes which move. The framing sentence for the day: your library is the vocabulary; today you get the sentence. Foreshadow the pain honestly — the judge at the end of today will call a mission and then change it, and squads whose plan is a pasted block will lose minutes where a list squad loses seconds. That’s the break-it, and it’s also exactly what the Surprise Rule does at a real WRO table.

title: The Setlist
text:
Unplugged: the pigeonholes 📮

Six numbered boxes on the bench, a pile of colored bricks. “Red into box 0. Blue into box 2. What’s in box 1? Swap 0 and 3. Add a green one at the end. Which box did it land in?”



You just used every list skill: a numbered row of slots, filled in order, counting from 0. Read a slot by its number (index), walk the row front to back (iterate), grow it at the end (append). Python calls this row a list, and you already think this way.



Run it physically before any code — 5 minutes, real boxes (or taped squares) and real bricks, quick-fire calls. The two stumbles to engineer on purpose: (1) “box 1” when they expect counting from 1 — let someone grab the wrong brick, then name the rule: robots count from 0; (2) append lands at the end, position = old length. Keep the boxes on the bench all day — every list question later gets answered by pointing at them. This is WRO-Learn’s arrays intro compressed into a game.

title: The Setlist
text:
Break it: the pasted plan 🔥

The judge calls: cross the stage · face the band · square on the wall. You paste it as one block. Then: “Actually, wall square FIRST.” How long does the edit take?

# mission_friday.py -- one pasted block 😬
drive_straight(400)          # cross the stage
robot.turn(90, absolute=True)   # face the band
drive_to_wall()
wall_square()         # reset at the wall
# judge: "wall square FIRST, then cross"…
# select lines… which? cut… paste… 🐛


The plan is trapped in the code. Reordering means surgery: select, cut, paste, and pray you moved all the lines of each step. Under a 5-minute clock, surgery loses. The plan needs to be a thing you can shuffle, like cards in a deck.



Let a squad actually attempt the live edit under a visible countdown — the fumble is the lesson. Diagnose together: the steps are clear in their heads (“cross”, “face”, “square”) but the code has no such boundaries; a step is 1–3 loose lines with nothing holding them together. Two missing ideas, teased in order: give each step a name (they own def — this is a two-minute step), then put the names in a row that can be shuffled — the pigeonholes from the warm-up. Don’t show the fix yet.

title: The Setlist
text:
Lists in sixty seconds
setlist = ["intro", "solo", "finale"]   # a numbered row of slots
setlist[0]                # "intro" -- count from 0, like the boxes!
setlist.append("encore")  # grows at the end → slot 3
setlist[1] = "duet"       # swap what a slot holds
for song in setlist:      # visit every slot, front to back
    print(song)


Index · append · iterate: the three moves from the pigeonhole game, now in Python. A list holds anything: strings, numbers, and (next slide) something sneakier. 😏



Type it live in the REPL, mirroring each line back to the physical boxes on the bench (“slot 0… that box”). Off-by-one and negative index (setlist[-1] = last box) are fun 30-second asides if the room is quick. Don’t linger — the payoff slide is next, and lists only get interesting once functions go inside them.

title: The Setlist
section: Steps are just functions: hold the name, don’t play it
text:
Steps are just functions: hold the name, don’t play it
def cross_stage():
    drive_straight(400)

def face_band():
    robot.turn(90, absolute=True)

def reset_at_wall():
    drive_to_wall(); wall_square()

mission = [reset_at_wall, cross_stage, face_band]
#          ^ no parentheses -- cards in a deck, not moves happening


cross_stage() plays the move. cross_stage, with no parentheses, is the recipe card itself: a thing you can hold, hand around, and drop into a list. A list of names is a setlist, the whole show before it has started.



This is the day’s one genuinely new idea — a function is a value. Land it with the recipe-card metaphor from the first def day: the card vs cooking the dish. Common bug to demo on purpose: write mission = [cross_stage(), face_band()] — the robot drives while the list is being built (the moves happen at line 10!) and the list ends up holding three Nones. Let them see that, then delete the parentheses. Note the judge’s reorder is now already solved on line 10 — reset_at_wall simply moved to slot 0.

title: The Setlist
text:
The runner, the whole thing
def run_mission(steps):
    for step in steps:   # take the next card…
        step()           # …now play it
run_mission(mission)


Three lines, and they never change again. Reorder the show → edit the list. Insert a step → append or slot it in. The judge changes the mission, and you change data, not code. That’s the split the pros live by.



Read it aloud in pigeonhole language: for each box front to back, take the card out, play it. The deep point — worth saying explicitly, once: the runner is control and the mission is data, and everything that changes lives in the data. This exact runner drives the anchor run in Week 3; per-step timeouts and a transition log are its stretch upgrade (the exemplar’s run_mission_logged) — offer to fast squads at the gate, never gate on it. A non-blocking state machine is continuation-season material; RoboMission runs are sequential, blocking is right.

title: The Setlist
text:
Setlist 🎵






The challenge


The judge calls a 3-step mini-mission, and you have 5 minutes to encode it as a mission list over your own library and run it. Score = steps completed, tiebreak = time.




Hear the mission → say it as verbs (“that’s a drive_straight, a robot.turn, a wall_square”) → wrap, list, run.
The judge will change the order on round two. 😈 Your surgery-free edit is the whole advantage.
Fast squads: swap in run_mission_logged, a per-step stopwatch plus a printed transition log.


Score decomposition, not typing speed: the squads to praise are the ones who translate the judge’s sentence into library verbs before touching a keyboard. Round two’s reorder is the day’s thesis under pressure — a list squad edits one line; watch for anyone still cutting and pasting blocks and coach them on the spot. The logged runner is the exemplar’s stretch (timeouts + transition log) — offer it, never gate it. Coach’s private scorecard today: list fluency, decomposition into verbs, debugging a sequence (which step failed? the log says).

title: The Setlist
text:
Today’s gate






You’re done today when…


You can read and build a list (index from 0, iterate, append), your steps are named functions over your own library, and the three-line runner walks a judge-called 3-step mission, with a reorder costing you one edit instead of surgery.




Next: the runner stops being a demo and becomes the anchor run. Your mechanism verbs join the list, and the chain starts paying points. 🤝


The gate is the plan’s D16 outcome verbatim. Sequencing note: this content was authored for D9 and deferred to D16 — by now the teams formed at Draft Day (D10) and the mechanisms are built, so the runner arrives with real verbs to call — drive_straight, robot.turn, claw.grab(), claw.let_go() — rather than as an abstract exercise. Note what the steps are not called: there is no push_cable() or place_mic() to drop into the list (#60), so the cable and the mic each arrive as a short run of ordinary verbs. That is the day’s thesis paying off rather than a gap — a list whose entries are mission-named wrappers reorders just as easily but reads like a black box, and the judge’s round-two change is exactly the moment a student needs to see what each step does. Say that out loud: the list they build today is the anchor run’s actual spine, not a rehearsal. Make sure every team’s movements.py + gripper files are saved and named before the chaining days.

title: Line King
text:
Where we left off



You own
Built on




📦 movements.py begins
drive_straight · turn


📈 error × KP
the turn · the straight


🛑 D, damping
brakes before overshoot










One thing up front


A script is blind. Today: see → decide → steer. Brightness only, colour names come in Week 4.




⏱️ Time: 5 minutes, then a bug hunt

Anchor today in what they already own, or it feels like a brand-new mountain (it isn’t — the plan flags the line day as the longest precisely because the old material was video-paced; live, it’s one formula applied a third time). Recap error × KP from the gyro out loud. Today the robot opens its eyes — three new powers land: the color eye (reflection = the echo of its own light), the per-surface threshold, and if (the first real decision). Flag the reflection-vs-color point early and firmly — kids will want to “detect the green line”; stop that now, it’s brightness only until Week 4. The day is eye → threshold → if → bang-bang → P on the line, then junction squaring — the P follower + squaring pair is the gate (it’s what the anchor run actually uses); the PD upgrade is the stretch for squads that tune P early. Two moves only: hard left or hard right. Predict the path.

while True:

Two answers means it can never go straight. It slams left-right forever.

The diagnosis you want in their words: “it only knows left or right, so it’s always turning.” The bridge to P is exactly the KP quiz from Day 4: what if the correction were proportional to how far off we are, instead of always full-tilt? title: Line King
text:

error = left_eye.reflection() - THRESHOLD    # signed: how far off the edge?
left.run(LINE_SPEED + KP * error)            # far → hard steer,
right.run(LINE_SPEED - KP * error)           # near → gentle


error × KP again. Tune KP: too small = lazy, too big = the wobble is back.



The “aha” is that they’ve written this line before — twice. It’s literally the D4 self-healing straight with a new error source: swap hub.imu.heading() for the eye’s reflection and the two run lines are identical. Same error × KP, different sensor feeding it. Two failure modes to name so they recognize them on the bench: sluggish (KP too low) drifts wide on curves; twitchy (KP too high) reintroduces the wobble. Start small and adjust. This alone wins “Line King” on gentle lines — but push the speed up on a curve and it starts to overshoot, which is the doorway to the PD stretch. If a student raises the “use motor.dc()” advice here: same answer as the D4 proportional-turn coach note — run() keeps “speed” meaning speed, so KP * error stays a correction in deg/s they can reason about.

section: Name it: follow_line joins the library 📦
text:
Name it: follow_line joins the library 📦
def follow_line(distance_mm, speed=250, kd=0):
    """P follow on the LEFT eye. kd > 0 is the PD stretch."""
    finish = left.angle() + distance_mm * DEG_PER_MM
    last_error = 0
    while left.angle() < finish:
        error = left_eye.reflection() - THRESHOLD
        steer = KP_LINE * error + kd * (error - last_error)
        left.run(speed + steer)
        right.run(speed - steer)
        last_error = error
        wait(10)
    left.stop(); right.stop()


The P loop, bottled. A finish line in degrees makes it a segment, and kd is the stretch knob.



Same promotion ritual as every day this week: the loose P loop gets a name and moves into movements.py (its KP becomes KP_LINE — the library’s constants block already owns KP for the gyro). Map every part back to what they own: error = P on the eye, the finish line = drive_straight’s DEG_PER_MM trick (follow for a distance — that’s how missions call it), kd * (error - last_error) = the D from the library-day gyro turn, with last_error the one-line memory that makes D possible. The gate is the P version — follow_line(600) with kd=0; the stretch is sliding kd up until the fast curve stops overshooting, which is what wins Speed Demon. State the I-policy plainly and move on: integral fixes a steady offset over a long run; our segments are short, so I is a demo they can watch but never something the gate depends on.

title: Line King
text:
The two-eye job: square up 📐
The second eye’s moment: you hit a junction crooked, so sit square before the next move.
def square_on_line(speed=160):
    """Stop each wheel as ITS OWN eye reaches the line."""
    left_done = right_done = False
    left.run(speed); right.run(speed)
    while not (left_done and right_done):
        if not left_done and left_eye.reflection() < THRESHOLD:
            left.hold(); left_done = True      # park left wheel
        if not right_done and right_eye.reflection() < THRESHOLD:
            right.hold(); right_done = True    # park right wheel
        wait(5)


Each eye stops its own wheel, so the robot pivots square. That’s why it carries two.




👁️ One eye can’t do this, and it’s worth knowing why. One reading tells you that you are on the line. It never tells you whether you’re crooked on it: a robot 20° askew and a robot dead square give the same number.




So a one-eye robot squares on a wall instead. Both wheels press the same flat edge, and the edge does the aligning. Two eyes square on a line, anywhere on the mat. That’s the trade the spare port buys.



Answer the port question head-on, and answer it with our robot, not the kit: the eye is on D, the two grippers take E and C, the drive motors F and B — which leaves exactly one spare port, A. Following needs one eye; this verb wants two. So the second eye is a purchase, and A is the money. Say what it costs: spend A on an eye and you can never add a third mechanism — though the 4-motor cap (§5.2.8) was going to stop you anyway. On the real mat this kills accumulated drift in a fraction of a second, gold going into the chained runs of Week 3. (The same second eye later reads note colours in Week 4 — but never steers.)

On the mat it erases accumulated drift in a fraction of a second, right before the next move — cheap, automatic insurance the chained runs of Week 3 lean on.

title: Line King
text:
Line King 👑 / Speed Demon 🏁






The challenge


Line King: hold the curved line for 30 s, on accuracy and speed. Speed Demon (fast squads): the fastest run that never leaves the line.





The winning recipe

Calibrate on the mat you run on
Tune KP_LINE, then chase speed
Square at the junction to reset
(stretch) kd kills the curve overshoot


Where squads lose it

Threshold from last week’s tape, not this mat 😬
KP so high the straight wobbles
Skipping the square → drift compounds



Line King rewards a clean, honest tune over raw speed; Speed Demon is the stretch for squads whose P was solid early and who took the kd upgrade. Coach’s eye is on the tuning conversation, not the trophy: can they explain what the error means, what KP_LINE did, and why the threshold had to be re-measured on this mat? That explanation IS the gate (kd talk is stretch credit, not a requirement). Keep the taped junction handy so squaring gets used under pressure, not just demoed.

One eye: you can show why it can’t, because crooked and square read the same, and the job carries to tomorrow’s wall
follow_line lives in your movements.py (it gains kd= for the PD stretch)





Next: Stop at the Wall. The motor becomes a sensor, and the wall resets the truth. 🧱


The gate is the plan’s line-day outcome: build, tune, and explain a P follower + reliable junction squaring — what the anchor run actually uses. Split the squaring half by build, because our competition robot runs one eye and square_on_line genuinely needs two: a two-eye squad demonstrates the verb, a one-eye squad demonstrates the failure (park it crooked on the line, read the number, park it square, read the same number) and carries the job to tomorrow, where wall_square solves it on the border. Do not fail a one-eye squad for a sensor it was never given. The heading= argument is tomorrow’s idea too — declaring a heading is D7’s “the wall never lies”, so name it, don’t teach it today; PD is explicitly the stretch, never the gate. A student who can narrate why each term is there owns the concept and can debug it in Week 3 when the follower serves the run. Two eyes, one job each: one follows, both square. Close by pointing forward: tomorrow the motor itself becomes a sensor — the robot feels walls, patrols between them, and resets its heading truth against them — and the scoresheet gets read the anchor-first way: everything those color-free verbs score comes first.

turn right

title: Plan the Path
text:
Quick quiz 🚨

Your route says turn right 90, four times, around a rectangle. Each turn lands 3° hot. Where is the robot pointing at the end?



12° off, and it stays 12° off. Nothing in the plan ever measures the mistake, so nothing can give it back. The fourth side is driving into the weeds.




You met this exact bug on the square day. 🧠 The cure was the same then: stop saying turn 90 more, start saying face 90.



This is a callback, not new material — the blind square from Drive a Square failed for precisely this reason, and the “targets that climb” payoff at the end of that day is the fix. Make them say the number: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, and the plan has no place to notice. Then land the sentence that runs the rest of the day: a relative turn banks its mistake; an absolute turn hands it back. If a squad protests “but I’d just tune the 90 to 87” — excellent, take it seriously, then ask what happens when the batteries drop and the scrub changes. Tuning a relative turn fixes one mat on one day.

section: The word you can’t write down ✍️
text:
The word you can’t write down ✍️

“Turn right” is not an instruction. It’s an instruction plus a secret: where you were already pointing.
turn_right(90)        # 90 from... where? the plan doesn't say
robot.turn(90, absolute=True)   # face 90. no secret.



A plan full of relative turns can only be read in order, from the start. Miss one step, and every number after it is wrong. 😬



Push on the “in order, from the start” line — it is the practical cost and they will feel it within the hour. With relative turns you cannot start a run in the middle to test one segment, you cannot reorder two jobs to save time, and you cannot debug step 7 without running steps 1 through 6. All three of those are things they will want to do today. Absolute headings make every step independently testable, which is the real reason the competition code uses them; error-absorption is the bonus.

Yaw tolerance is ±31°, which is generous. A rough approach still scores if it aims at the right heading. Paste 100 straight into robot.turn(…, absolute=True) and you’re 90° out: sideways, and 128 mm won’t fit in 79.7. 💸



Land the arithmetic slowly — 190 and 170 are both ±10 from 180, which is straight down the mat, and that is the sanity check they should run on every converted number: does the answer point somewhere the mat actually agrees with? The ±31° tolerance is the good news and the trap in one figure: it is wide enough to forgive a sloppy drive, which is why a 90° frame error is so nasty — it is far outside tolerance, so it never half-works and never teaches you gradually. It just fails, cleanly, at 15 points. Tie it back to the anchor: cables are 30 of the ~135, and half of 30 is the difference between a gate that passes and one that doesn’t.

section: So the step has to name a heading
text:
So the step has to name a heading

CABLE_UPPER_HEADING = 190     # facts about the MAT
CABLE_LOWER_HEADING = 170

robot.turn(CABLE_UPPER_HEADING, absolute=True)   # …then push



Two cables, two numbers, one step shape: not one number, and not two copies
The heading is a fact about the mat, so it lives with the other mat facts




Try writing this with a relative turn. You can’t, because “turn 20” only means something if you already know where you were. The mat doesn’t care where you were. 🤷



This closes the loop opened in section B: the circled “turn right” phrases on the board are now provably unwritable for this job. The design point for the stronger squads is that the two cables differ by a number, not by a behaviour — same lesson as drive_straight(distance_mm) — so the number gets a name and the step gets written once in shape. Do not let anyone paste 190 into one place and 170 into a near-identical copy of the same block; a bare 190 in the middle of a mission is a magic number that nobody will find when the mat is re-measured, and a second copy is the habit the constants block was built to kill. If a squad proposes wrapping the turn-and-push into push_cable(heading), say the honest thing: that is a good instinct and it is deferred, not wrong. Three lines that appear twice do not yet earn a name in a 5-week course, and hiding the mission behind mission-named verbs is what stops a student reading their own run; composing verbs is a continuation-season job (decision #60). What they must take away today is the heading, which is worth 15 points and cannot be recovered later.

title: Plan the Path
text:
Lab: draw the anchor run 🖍️

On your mat printout, mark every one of these:

🏁 the origin and the zero direction (the same one your code will reset to)
📍 each job in order: instruments 45 · cables 30 · avoidance 40 · mic 20
🧭 the heading for every leg, tagged (map)
🩹 every reset point: a wall square or a line, where error goes back to zero




Rule of thumb from the optimizer: don’t dead-reckon more than about 3 m without erasing error somewhere. 🧽



Circulate with the printouts and hunt for three specific things. One: an unlabelled heading — ask “map or field?” and enjoy the pause. Two: a long stretch with no reset point, which is where their run will actually die on competition day. Three: a fragile step placed late, after points are already banked — the ordering principle is never put a shaky step where its failure costs points you already earned. The ~3 m figure comes from the optimizer’s dead-reckoning cap; it is a planning heuristic, not a hard rule, and squads with a well-tuned gyro will beat it. Time-box this hard at 25 minutes or it eats the session.

title: Plan the Path
text:
Competition: Cartographers 🗺️

The judge names a job on the mat. 90 seconds to hand back: the heading to face it (tagged), the distance in mm, and the nearest reset point you’d use.


Score: 1 point per correct number · +2 if the frame tag is right · −2 for an untagged heading 😈


Run three rounds so every squad gets a different job and nobody wins on one lucky memorised number. The −2 is deliberately harsh and you should announce it cheerfully — an untagged heading is worse than no heading, because the untagged one gets used. Judges: accept any heading within the ±31° yaw tolerance for cable jobs, and within ±10° elsewhere; you are scoring the plan, not their gyro. If a squad hands back a field-frame number correctly tagged (field) plus the conversion, that is full marks — the tag is the skill.

title: Plan the Path
text:
You’re done today when…






Gate


Your squad has a written path plan for the ~135 anchor run: every leg’s heading tagged with its frame, every distance in mm off the map, and every reset point marked. You can also convert a field_data.py heading to a robot heading without looking it up.




Next: the plan stops being paper. 🎵


The gate is a paper deliverable on purpose — no robot has to run for a squad to pass, which is what makes this day survivable when the hardware is misbehaving. Photograph every squad’s printout before they leave; those photos are the reference for the segment-integration sessions and they will lose the paper. Anyone who finishes early: hand them the Route mode of the tool and ask for a measured detour around an avoidance object with the 130 mm clearance respected — that is real work the run needs and it is genuinely hard to eyeball.
